note: Each point is a summary in this tool's own words of a published view. Forecasts are the sources' views, not facts, and some sources are firms with an interest in the outcome.

for.text: Data centers used about 4.4% of U.S. electricity in 2023, and the national lab's scenarios put that at roughly 7% to 12% by 2028.

source.name: U.S. Department of Energy, on Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory's 2024 data center energy report

for.text: One manager argues the bigger risk is that power and capacity arrive too slowly for demand, not that too much gets built.

source.name: Janus Henderson, Data center power: why the key risk is under-delivery, not overbuild

against.text: If AI demand grows more slowly than forecast, new capacity can sit idle. A PwC study of the Gulf region puts about $12 billion of data center investment at risk for each idle gigawatt.

source.name: PwC Strategy&, The gigawatt bubble

against.text: Analysts have warned that overbuilding becomes a real risk if AI adoption flattens or shifts, as happened with fiber in the dot-com era.

source.name: Data Center Knowledge, Analysts warn of overbuild risks as AI data centers reshape industry

for.text: Gartner expected worldwide software spending to grow about 15% in 2026, among the fastest-growing parts of IT.

source.name: Gartner, worldwide IT spending forecast, February 2026

for.text: Even lenders worried about AI don't expect the whole software market to collapse at once; they see pressure arriving gradually and unevenly, company by company.

source.name: RBC BlueBay, AI software disruption and credit markets

against.text: Private credit lent heavily to software: about $500 billion, roughly 19% of direct loans, by the end of 2025. Software stocks fell almost 30% between October 2025 and February 2026 on AI fears.

source.name: Bank for International Settlements, Private credit's software lending meets AI disruption (March 2026)

against.text: AI can hurt borrowers through lost revenue, thinner margins, lower valuations and harder refinancing, which makes the quality of each company and its owner matter more.

source.name: J.P. Morgan Asset Management, Disruption decoded

for.text: Most published estimates find the U.S. short of homes, by anywhere from about 1.5 million to 5.5 million depending on the method.

source.name: Congressional Research Service, Estimates of a "Housing Shortage" (December 2025)

for.text: One estimate has the gap growing, from about 3.8 million homes in 2024 to about 4.0 million in 2025.

source.name: Real Estate News, Deeply rooted housing shortage worsened in 2025 (Realtor.com estimate)

against.text: There's no universal agreement that a national shortage exists; estimates vary widely with their assumptions.

source.name: Congressional Research Service, Estimates of a "Housing Shortage" (December 2025)

against.text: After record apartment completions, apartment vacancy reached about 8.3% at the end of 2024, the highest since records began in 2000.

source.name: NMHC, Reconciling the apartment shortage with recent record apartment completions

for.text: National industrial vacancy fell below 7% in the second quarter of 2026, with leasing at its strongest pace since mid-2022.

source.name: Supply & Demand Chain Executive, on Cushman & Wakefield's Q2 2026 industrial report

for.text: New construction has slowed sharply: completions in early 2026 were the lowest since 2017, which helps demand catch up with supply.

source.name: Cushman & Wakefield, Peak industrial vacancy likely in rearview mirror (April 2026)

against.text: Another data provider measured national vacancy at about 9.1% in June 2026, with roughly 400 million square feet still under construction.

source.name: CRE Daily, US industrial vacancy and rent growth stabilize in June 2026 (Yardi Matrix)

against.text: Readings differ by about two points depending on who measures, so "tight" depends on whose data is used, and local markets vary more.

source.name: Supply & Demand Chain Executive, on Cushman & Wakefield's Q2 2026 industrial report

for.text: U.S. electricity use was forecast to rise four years in a row for the first time since 2007, the fastest four-year growth since 2000, driven mainly by large computing centers.

source.name: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Short-Term Energy Outlook release, January 2026

for.text: Developers are expected to rush solar projects ahead of tax-credit deadlines, adding about 36 gigawatts more by 2030 than previously expected.

source.name: S&P Global Market Intelligence, Impacts of H.R. 1 on renewable energy tax credits

against.text: After 2025's tax law cut wind and solar credits, one analysis has both below their earlier paths by 2035, by about 42 and 52 gigawatts.

source.name: S&P Global Market Intelligence, Impacts of H.R. 1 on renewable energy tax credits

against.text: Power plants and lines built for data centers can be stranded if that demand falls short, with costs often passed to ratepayers.

source.name: PwC Strategy&, The gigawatt bubble

for.text: National health spending is projected to reach about $9 trillion by 2034, rising from 18.4% to 20.6% of the economy.

source.name: Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, on CMS's 2025–2034 national health expenditure projections

for.text: An aging population makes Medicare the fastest-growing major payer, and drug use, including GLP-1 medicines, adds near-term growth.

source.name: ADvancing States, summary of National Health Expenditure Projections, 2025–34

against.text: Medicaid changes in recent legislation are projected to slow spending growth after 2026.

source.name: ADvancing States, summary of National Health Expenditure Projections, 2025–34

against.text: The share of Americans with health insurance is projected to dip, from 91.8% in 2024 to 90.5% in 2034.

source.name: HealthExec, on CMS's projection of $9 trillion in health spending by 2034
